newsitem.title: USA: U.S. immigration pledges no mass deportations.
newsitem.headline: U.S. immigration pledges no mass deportations.

text.p: U.S. immigration officials on Friday vowed there would be no mass deportations of immigrants and said they would wait for a ruling by a federal judge on a request for an injunction to halt such action.

The pledge could serve to ease the minds of thousands of Nicaraguans whose fear of deportation was heightened on Thursday when U.S. District Judge James Lawrence King said he could not immediately rule on the preliminary injunction.

King's decision allowed a temporary restraining order to expire at midnight on Thursday, effectively permitting the United States to resume the expulsion of Nicaraguans and other immigrants who have lived legally in the country for years.

King, who issued the restraining order in mid-May, urged the government not to take action against immigrants who could be legally deported and the Immigration and Naturalisation Service said on Friday it was heeding King's wishes.
"There will absolutely be no mass deportations," INS spokesman Brian Jordan said. "We are patiently awaiting the final decision of Judge King."
Jordan noted that there was nothing to stop INS from legally deporting immigrants but said the agency was aware of the sensitivity of the issue in the immigrant community.

"In the interim, there will be no depotations of non-criminals who have received final orders for deportation," he said. "However, if we encounter a criminal with an aggravated felony record, we shall consider that person for removal proceedings."

New immigration laws enacted in April left tens of thousands of Miami immigrants, primarily Nicaraguans who had lived legally in the United States for up to 10 years, fearing deportation to their homelands.

Immigration lawyers have said the new laws spread panic through the Miami Nicaraguan community, where families were moving from house to house to avoid capture and children were being pulled from schools.

Many Nicaraguans fled the 1980s civil war in their homeland and came to the United States at the urging of the U.S. government, then lived in legal limbo for years while buying homes, raising families and paying taxes.
Attorney Ira Kurzban, representing the immigrants in the class-action petition for an injunction, said he was not surprised by the INS decision to be patient.
"It enhances their position that there's no irreparable harm being done to the immigrants," Kurzban said. "It's a short-term strategic position."

Kurzban said he expected it would not take King more than a couple of weeks to rule and said patience on the part of the INS would enhance the agency's legal position should the case go to an appeals court.
